title: Family and friends guide
description: Plan a calm conversation, keep yourself safe, and hold on to family ties where you can.
intro: You do not have to tell everyone at once. This page helps you work out who actually needs to know, what to say in the first minute, and how to stop the conversation turning into a debate.
summary: Tell people when it is safe and there is a reason to, not because you feel rushed.
Keep the first conversation short, and keep it about you.
You can set a boundary without insulting your family or the people you grew up with.
If telling someone could put you in danger, talk to a trusted professional or a local support service first.

sections.heading: Before you tell someone
sections.body:
Start with what this particular person needs to know today. A parent you live with is not the same as a cousin you see twice a year, and a spouse is not the same as an old school friend. The amount of detail can be different for each of them.

If you depend on someone for housing, tuition, immigration paperwork, a ride to work, or your basic safety, think hard before you make a big announcement. Islam does not ask you to put yourself in danger to prove you are sincere.
items: Pick one calm person before you tell a whole room.
Choose a private moment. Not a birthday dinner, not the middle of an argument.
Know your one main point before you start talking.
Have somewhere you can go if the conversation turns hostile.

sections.heading: What to say first
sections.body: Lead with your own reasons and skip the lecture. Most families react out of fear: that you have changed, that they have lost you, or that the things they have heard about Islam are true. A short personal explanation usually lands better than a long argument.
items: Tell them you are still their child, their sibling, their friend.
Tell them Islam is helping you worship God and live with more purpose.
Say plainly that you are still learning.
If the first conversation stays respectful, invite them to ask you more later.

sections.heading: Setting limits without a fight
sections.body: A boundary is not a punishment. It is a line that protects your prayer, your dignity, or your safety. You can be gentle and still hold the line.
items: You can refuse to argue about Islam at the dinner table.
You can walk away when a conversation turns insulting.
You can ask people to stop mocking prayer, hijab, halal food, or the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
You can keep being kind to them and still refuse pressure to leave Islam.

sections.heading: Holidays, meals, and living at home
sections.body: Family routines will be awkward for a while. Keep two things in view: stay away from food that is clearly haram, and keep the relationship calm where you can. If a family event involves worship from another religion, ask a qualified local imam about your exact situation rather than guessing.
items: Offer to bring a dish you can eat.
Thank the people who make room for you.
Do not let every meal turn into a debate about halal details.
If you get pushed into something religiously confusing, ask a qualified person about it privately.

sections.heading: Safety comes first
sections.body: If someone might hurt you, stop you leaving, read your phone, take your documents, or put you out of the house, this is not a simple conversation. Before you say anything, contact a trusted local professional, a crisis line, a shelter, a counselor, a chaplain, or a community leader who understands safety planning.

scripts.title: If they are worried
scripts.body: I know this is a lot to hear, and I know it might scare you. I'm still me. I'm not asking you to understand all of it today. Islam is helping me worship God and be more deliberate about how I live. I'd just like us to keep talking without it turning into a fight.

scripts.title: If they want to argue
scripts.body: I love you, and I really don't want this to turn into an argument. I'm still learning, so I probably can't answer everything anyway. I can send you something to read later, or we can talk when we've both cooled off.

scripts.title: At a family meal
scripts.body: Thanks for including me. I don't eat pork or drink alcohol now, so I brought something I can eat as well. I still want to be here with everyone.

scenarios.title: A friend says you changed too fast.
scenarios.response: Agree that something changed, then say what has not: you still care about them, you still hold the values you shared, and you are not planning to cut anyone off.

scenarios.title: A parent asks if you rejected them.
scenarios.response: Tell them that becoming Muslim was not a vote against the family. Keep the conversation on worshipping God and becoming a better person rather than on what they did wrong.

scenarios.title: Someone threatens your safety.
scenarios.response: End the conversation if you can do that safely. Contact local emergency services, a trusted professional, or a safety support organization before you say anything else.

title: First masjid visit guide
description: What to expect the first time you walk into a masjid: what to wear, where your shoes go, who to ask for help, and how Friday prayer is different.
intro: Every masjid runs a little differently. The visit gets easier once you know who to ask, what to wear, and what to do when you cannot tell what is happening.
summary: You are allowed to phone or email the masjid before you go.
Clean and modest clothes are enough. You do not need cultural clothing.
When you get there, ask one person directly for help.
Friday prayer is much busier than a regular daily prayer.

sections.heading: Before you go
sections.body: Check the masjid website, or phone ahead if you can. Prayer times, which door to use, women's spaces, accessibility, parking, and support for new Muslims all differ from one masjid to the next.
items: Find the prayer time and plan to arrive 10 to 20 minutes early.
Bring socks if you would rather not be barefoot once your shoes are off.
Silence your phone before you step into the prayer area.
If you are nervous, ask whether someone can meet you at the door.

sections.heading: What to wear
sections.body: Wear clean, modest clothes you can bow and prostrate in. Cultural clothing is not required. If you are unsure, go loose with good coverage, and skip slogans or large images that might distract people who are praying.

sections.heading: When you walk in
sections.body: Most masjids have a shoe rack near the door. Some have separate prayer spaces or separate entrances for men and women. If you cannot tell which is which, stop near the entrance and ask.
items: Say it is your first visit and that you are new to Islam or still learning.
Ask where the shoes go and where you should sit.
Ask where people make wudu if you need to.
During prayer, line up with the rows and follow what the group does.

sections.heading: Friday prayer basics
sections.body: Jumu'ah is the Friday congregational prayer. There is a sermon first, then the prayer, and the room is usually full. If your first visit lands on a Friday, come early and expect the parking, the doors, and the seating to be crowded.

sections.heading: Women's space, accessibility, and support
sections.body: Women's spaces are not the same everywhere. Some are large and busy, some are small, and some open only for certain prayers. Accessibility and parking vary too. Asking before you visit is completely normal.
items: Is the women's prayer area open for this prayer?
Is there an accessible entrance or an elevator?
Where should a first-time visitor park?
Is there a class for new Muslims, a mentor, or someone I could talk to?

scripts.title: Calling or emailing ahead
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. I'm a new Muslim and I'd like to visit for the first time. Could you tell me which door to use, whether there's someone who looks after new Muslims, and if there's a particular prayer I should come for?

scripts.title: At the door
scripts.body: Assalamu alaykum. It's my first time here and I'm still learning. Could you show me where to leave my shoes and where I should sit?

scripts.title: Asking about support for new Muslims
scripts.body: Do you have a class for new Muslims, or someone who helps beginners with prayer and the basics?

scenarios.title: No one notices you.
scenarios.response: Do not read that as a rejection. People are usually rushing to make the prayer. Pick one person and ask them for exactly what you need.

scenarios.title: Someone corrects you abruptly.
scenarios.response: Take whatever is useful in it and let the tone go. One blunt person is not Islam and is not the whole community. If the correction sounded important, ask someone calmer about it later.

scenarios.title: The masjid cannot offer convert support.
scenarios.response: Ask whether they know another masjid, a chaplain, a class, or a community group nearby. Support can come from a different mosque, an online class, or one steady person.

title: Work and school guide
description: Practical wording for prayer, fasting and food at work or school, and which accommodation rules apply where you are in Canada.
intro: Most of this gets easier if you ask early and keep the request small and specific. You do not owe anyone your whole life story to get a few minutes for prayer.
summary: Work out where prayer fits in your real schedule before you ask anyone to change anything.
When you do need something, ask for something small and specific, and put it in writing.
Which rules apply depends on your employer: federally regulated workplaces follow the Canadian Human Rights Act, and everyone else follows the law of their province or territory.
Quebec has extra rules for some public-sector jobs and public places. They changed in 2026.
This page is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Start with your real schedule
sections.body: Write down your shifts or class times, your breaks, your commute, and any clean quiet space nearby. Most prayers fit into an ordinary break once you can see it on paper. For the ones that do not, a short specific request lands better than a long explanation about religion.

sections.heading: Prayer at work or school
sections.body: Depending on the season, up to three of the five prayers can fall in a 9 to 5 day. Each one usually takes 10 to 15 minutes, including wudu. The prayer itself is short. Walking somewhere and getting back to your desk take the rest.
items: Use the breaks you already have where you can.
Wudu can be done at an ordinary washroom sink.
A clean, quiet, private spot is enough. It does not need to be a special room.
Keep a small prayer mat or a clean cloth in your bag if that helps.
Do not pray in a walkway, an in-use classroom, or anywhere unsafe on a worksite.
If your work makes prayer timing genuinely hard, ask an imam about it.

sections.heading: Friday prayer, Ramadan and Eid
sections.body: Jumu'ah and Ramadan take more planning, so ask before the schedule is locked in. Jumu'ah usually needs at least an hour away from work, including travel. In Ramadan you might ask to work through lunch and leave a little early, or for less physical work if your role allows it. For Eid, Ontario's guidance says forcing you to use vacation days instead of looking at other options, such as lieu time or a shift swap, would likely be discriminatory.

sections.heading: What to hand your manager
sections.body: A short written request saves a lot of back and forth. Say which prayers fall in your hours, roughly when, how long each takes, where you could pray, and how you will make up the time.
items: The Managers Guide to supporting Muslim Employees, a short job aid written by a network of Muslim federal employees, explains prayer times, wudu and space in plain terms. It is not official government policy, but managers find it useful.
The NCCM guide Know Your Rights and Responsibilities lists the accommodations Muslim employees and students often ask for. It dates from 2019, so check anything legal against the current rules.
If you work somewhere federally regulated, the Canadian Human Rights Commission suggests putting the accommodation plan in writing, signed by everyone involved.

sections.heading: Which rules apply to you
sections.body: Which law applies depends on who your employer is, not only on where you live.
items: Federally regulated workplaces: federal departments and agencies, First Nations governments, banks, Crown corporations such as Canada Post, broadcasting, and air and rail transport follow the Canadian Human Rights Act. The Canadian Human Rights Commission describes four steps: talk, assess, accommodate, then review. A complaint to the Commission has to be made within one year of the last discriminatory act.

Ontario: the Ontario Human Rights Commission's creed policy says employers and schools must accommodate a sincerely held religious practice unless it causes undue hardship, which is limited to cost, outside funding, and health and safety. You do not have to prove a practice is required in Islam. Give reasonable notice and help look for a solution. Small amounts of prayer time should not cost you pay.
Alberta: the Alberta Human Rights Commission lists religious beliefs as a ground employers must accommodate at work.
British Columbia: the BC Human Rights Code protects religion, as the BC Human Rights Tribunal explains.
Other provinces and territories each have their own human rights commission or tribunal. We have not yet checked their pages, so look yours up on your provincial or territorial government's website.

sections.heading: Quebec: public-sector rules in 2026
sections.body: Quebec's Act respecting the laicity of the State was amended by Bill 9, An Act respecting the reinforcement of laicity in Quebec, which received assent on April 2, 2026 (Statutes of Quebec 2026, chapter 6). The consolidated law, up to date as of September 1, 2026, says the following. Last checked September 23, 2026.
items: People in the roles the law lists may not wear religious symbols, such as a hijab, while working. The list includes principals, vice principals and teachers in school service centres, peace officers, school staff who work with students, and staff of subsidised childcare and daycare centres.
Religious practice, including prayer, is not allowed in places run by the public bodies the law lists. There are exceptions, such as health centres, correctional facilities and private homes.
The law lists CEGEPs and universities among those bodies, so it may affect campus prayer rooms. Ask your campus or a lawyer before you rely on this.
Overt prayer is not allowed in subsidised private schools during class hours.
The law uses the notwithstanding clause. The Supreme Court of Canada heard a challenge in March 2026. We have not checked whether it has ruled.
If you are in Quebec, check the current law or talk to a legal clinic before you make a job or study decision.

sections.heading: Food and work socials
sections.body: Your coworkers do not need a lesson on halal certification. A plain sentence covers it.
items: I don't eat pork and I don't drink.
I eat halal meat, but vegetarian or seafood is usually easiest when we're ordering as a group.
Don't worry if that's awkward, I'm happy to bring my own food.

sections.heading: A legal note
sections.body: This is general information, not legal advice. Laws and policies change, and every school and employer handles requests differently. For your own situation, contact the human rights commission where you live, a legal clinic, or a lawyer.

scripts.title: Asking for a prayer break
scripts.body: There's a prayer I need to do in the afternoon and it takes about ten minutes. Could I take my break around then and use a quiet clean spot where I won't be in anyone's way?

scripts.title: Asking about Fridays
scripts.body: On Fridays there's a congregational prayer around midday. Could we talk about whether I can shift my lunch break, or make the time up somewhere else in the week?

scripts.title: A short written request
scripts.body: As a Muslim, I pray at set times. During my shift, one or two prayers fall around [times], and each takes about ten minutes. I'd like to use my break for them, or take a few minutes and make them up at the end of the day. A quiet corner or empty room would work. Happy to talk through what suits the team.

scripts.title: Talking to someone at school
scripts.body: I'm Muslim and I need a few minutes to pray during the day. Who should I talk to about a suitable space and about fitting it around my schedule?

scenarios.title: You are embarrassed to ask.
scenarios.response: Lead with one practical need. Asking about a break does not require you to tell anyone your conversion story.

scenarios.title: Your manager says no immediately.
scenarios.response: Stay calm and ask who handles accommodation or scheduling requests, then put your request in writing. If it still goes nowhere, check the human rights commission that covers your workplace, or speak to a legal clinic.

scenarios.title: A work social is built around drinking.
scenarios.response: Only go if you can hold your own boundaries there. Where you can, suggest coffee, lunch, or something else instead.

title: Identity and culture guide
description: Be Muslim without feeling you have to take on somebody else's culture.
intro: Islam changes how you worship and what you value. It does not wipe out your personality, your ethnicity, your language, or the good parts of where you come from.
summary: You do not have to become Arab, South Asian, African, Turkish, or anything else to be Muslim.
Changing your name is usually not required, unless the name itself means something clearly bad or against Islamic belief.
Feeling lonely, or stuck between two cultures, is common for converts.
Good company helps you grow without asking you to perform an identity.

sections.heading: Islam and culture
sections.body: Islam came for every people and every place. Muslim communities carry culture with them: food, clothing, language, family customs, humor, manners. Some of that is beautiful. Some of it is just how things are done in one town. You can learn from people without assuming that every habit you see is a religious rule.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: Most new Muslims keep the name they were given. Some add a Muslim name because they want to. A change is usually not required unless the name conflicts with Islamic belief or means something ugly. If you are not sure what your name means, ask someone qualified rather than assuming the worst.

sections.heading: The in-between feeling
sections.body: You can end up feeling too Muslim for your old circles and too new for Muslim ones. That feeling is real, and it is not evidence that you made the wrong choice. It usually means your life is still rearranging itself.
items: Build one or two steady Muslim friendships instead of chasing a whole crowd.
Keep the non-Muslim friendships where your faith gets respected.
Look for classes where beginner questions are normal.
Step away from online spaces that leave you feeling permanently behind.

sections.heading: When people pile it on
sections.body: Plenty of people give good advice at the wrong time. You can thank them for caring and still set your own pace. The foundations come first: belief, prayer, character, the basics of halal, and a reliable place to learn.

sections.heading: Signs you are in good company
items: They explain the basics without making you feel stupid.
They point you towards qualified teachers.
They take your family situation and your safety seriously.
They do not try to cut you off from everyone who knew you before Islam.
They can say I do not know when a question needs a scholar.

scripts.title: When someone says you need a new culture
scripts.body: I'm glad to learn from Muslim cultures, but I'm also trying to work out what Islam itself actually asks of me. I want to grow in a way I can keep up.

scripts.title: When someone pushes you to change your name
scripts.body: From what I've learned, changing my name isn't automatically required. I might think about it later. Right now I'm putting my effort into prayer and the basics.

scripts.title: When you feel behind
scripts.body: I'm new and I am taking this seriously. Could you help me with what matters most right now instead of giving me ten things at once?

scenarios.title: You are the only convert in the room.
scenarios.response: Look for one sincere person instead of trying to belong to everybody at once. Being new is not a defect.

scenarios.title: People confuse culture with Islam.
scenarios.response: Ask it plainly: is this a religious requirement, a recommended practice, or a local custom?

scenarios.title: Old friends think Islam erased you.
scenarios.response: Let your character answer that over time. You can tell them Islam is guiding you, not deleting your history.

title: Relationships and marriage basics
description: Slow the big decisions down, ask the right people, and protect your safety and your dignity.
intro: Relationships get complicated after the Shahada, especially where family, a dating history, marriage pressure, or a partner's expectations are in the mix. The first step here is simple: do not make a rushed decision about your life on your own.
summary: Marriage, divorce, custody, being pushed to convert for a marriage, and family conflict all need qualified local guidance.
You do not have to settle every relationship question in your first few weeks as a Muslim.
Boundaries are part of your dignity. They are not evidence of weak faith.
If there are threats, control, violence, immigration pressure, or money you depend on, talk to a safety professional or a trusted local service before you act.

sections.heading: What can wait
sections.body: You can learn to pray, find your feet in a community, and sort out halal basics without settling your entire marriage future this month. If someone is pushing you to marry, divorce, move, change your finances, or cut off your family quickly, stop and get qualified help.
items: Do not marry someone because you feel you owe them for helping you become Muslim.
Do not hide the legal, safety, or money side of it from the people advising you.
Do not let comments online decide a marriage or a divorce.
Do not let shame push you into a decision you do not understand.

sections.heading: Before a serious decision
sections.body: Write the actual situation down in plain words. Say whether you live together, whether children are involved, whether there is pressure or fear in it, and whether legal documents, immigration status, debts, or your housing are affected.
items: Ask what Islam requires, what it recommends, and what can wait.
Ask whether your situation needs a local scholar, a counselor, a lawyer, or a safety service.
If a civil marriage or divorce is already in motion, ask both a religious and a legal professional what applies to you.
If you feel unsafe, sort out safety planning first and leave the religious debate for later.

sections.heading: How to ask an imam
sections.body: A clear question lets an imam or teacher answer responsibly. Tell them you are a new Muslim and that you want a practical next step, not a full legal manual.
items: What is the immediate religious priority in my situation?
Does this need a private appointment instead of a quick answer in the hallway?
Should I also speak to a counselor, a lawyer, a mediator, or a safety service?
Are there details I should not share publicly?

sections.heading: Boundaries and safety
sections.body: Religious language does not make a relationship healthy. Watch for pressure, being cut off from other people, threats, someone checking your phone, someone controlling the money, a rush to marry, or being told you may not ask anyone else for advice.

sections.heading: This is not legal or marriage counseling
sections.body: This page is general education. It cannot tell you whether a marriage is valid, whether a divorce took effect, whether a custody arrangement is safe, or what your legal rights are. For anything personal, use qualified local help.

scripts.title: Asking for time
scripts.body: I'm new to this and I want to get it right rather than fast. I'm going to ask a qualified local imam first, and a counselor or a lawyer if I need one, before I decide anything.

scripts.title: Asking an imam
scripts.body: I'm a new Muslim and I need advice about a relationship. There may be marriage, family pressure, and safety involved. Could I book a private time so I can explain it properly?

scripts.title: Holding a boundary
scripts.body: I want to handle this in a halal and respectful way, but I'm not okay with being pressured. I need time, and I need proper advice.

scenarios.title: Someone says you must marry quickly now that you are Muslim.
scenarios.response: Stop there. Marriage is worship and it is also a legal decision about the rest of your life. Ask a qualified local imam and someone you trust before you agree to anything.

scenarios.title: A partner uses Islam to control who you talk to.
scenarios.response: Good advice never cuts you off from qualified help. Speak privately with a trusted imam, a counselor, or a safety professional.

scenarios.title: You are already married and your spouse is not Muslim.
scenarios.response: Do not settle this with general content off a website. Ask a qualified local scholar who can go through your actual situation with you.

title: Loneliness and belonging
description: Build one steady connection, and know when it is time for professional help.
intro: A lot of new Muslims feel caught between two worlds for a while. Loneliness is not proof that your faith is weak. It usually means your friendships, your routines, and the places you belong are all changing at once.
summary: Belonging usually starts with one or two steady people rather than a room full of acquaintances.
Keep the non-Muslim friendships where your faith gets respected.
A small weekly routine takes the pressure off deciding everything fresh each day.
If the loneliness turns into hopelessness, panic, thoughts of hurting yourself, or not being able to function, get help straight away: call or text 9-8-8, or call 911 in an emergency.

sections.heading: This kind of loneliness is real
sections.body: You may feel too Muslim for some of your old places and too new for some Muslim ones. It hurts, and it is common enough that it should be said out loud instead of hidden. In a 2025 Yaqeen Institute survey of 618 converts in the United States, about 40% said they felt lonely during Ramadan and 42% on Eid. The sample was American, not Canadian, but you are clearly not the only one. New Muslim Academy puts it simply: communities are made of human beings, and human beings are imperfect.
items: Not knowing every custom does not put you behind.
Missing parts of your old routine does not make you a fake.
One awkward masjid visit does not mean you are on your own.
You can build this slowly without pretending it is easy.

sections.heading: Build one steady connection
sections.body: Find one reliable person before you go looking for a crowd. That might be a calm class teacher, a convert mentor, a chaplain, a Muslim coworker, or whoever at the masjid answers basic questions kindly. In the same survey, 78% of converts said they made friends at their local mosque.

sections.heading: Convert programmes in Canada
sections.body:
Some Canadian masjids run programmes made for new Muslims. A few examples, each described on the organisation's own website: Convert Care at Islam Care Centre in Ottawa, every Wednesday at 6:00 pm; Convert Connect at MAC Masjid Toronto, which can arrange a guide for your first visit; the New Muslim Family Meet Up at London Muslim Mosque; weekly revert meet-ups at Ummah Masjid in Halifax; the Converts Committee at the Manitoba Islamic Association in Winnipeg; and New Muslim Care at the BC Muslim Association. The community topic lists more, with their websites.

Confirm before you go. Times and places change, and we last checked these on 23 September 2026.

sections.heading: A gentle weekly routine
items: Get to one prayer, class, or community event when you can.
Send one message to someone you trust instead of going quiet.
Keep one good non-Muslim friendship going.
Get off your phone for a while when the online arguments make Islam feel heavy.

sections.heading: When to get professional help
sections.body: Spiritual support and clinical support work fine together. If you feel unsafe, cannot sleep or function, are stuck in panic, or are at risk of hurting yourself, reach out now. In an emergency, call 911. If you are thinking about suicide or are worried about someone, call or text 9-8-8 at any time (988.ca). A clinician or a faith-aware counsellor can help with the longer road.

sections.heading: Do not measure belonging by noise
sections.body: Some people find community quietly. You will not be invited to everything, and that stings. Even so, one honest class, one respectful friend, and one steady dua will carry you further than a long list of shallow contacts.

scripts.title: Asking for one connection
scripts.body: I'm a new Muslim and I'm trying to find some steady support. Is there one class, mentor, or person you'd point me to?

scripts.title: Texting when you feel isolated
scripts.body: I've been pretty lonely lately and I'm trying not to just disappear. Could we catch up sometime this week, even for ten minutes?

scripts.title: Asking for professional support
scripts.body: I'm struggling with loneliness and it's getting in the way of my day. Could you help me find a counselor, a crisis line, or mental health support that understands faith?

scenarios.title: You went to the masjid and no one greeted you.
scenarios.response: Try not to let one visit stand for the whole place. People are often busy or shy. Ask one person for the new Muslim contact or the class.

scenarios.title: Old friends invite you somewhere uncomfortable.
scenarios.response: Suggest somewhere else. You can keep the friendship and still change what you do together.

scenarios.title: Loneliness is turning into despair.
scenarios.response: Take that seriously. Call or text 9-8-8 today, talk to a clinician or someone you trust, or call 911 if you are in danger.

title: Signs of a healthy community
description: Tell the difference between support that helps you grow and pressure dressed up as help.
intro: A good Muslim community makes the basics easier to carry. This page lists what decent support looks like, and the warning signs that mean you should step back or get qualified help.
summary: A healthy community takes beginner questions in stride and knows when to send you to someone qualified.
Good support respects your family situation, your safety, your privacy, and the fact that you are growing gradually.
Pressure, isolation, secrecy, and shame are the warning signs.
One difficult person does not stand for the whole Muslim community.

sections.heading: Good signs
items: They answer basic questions without laughing at you.
They can say I do not know, and then point you to someone who does.
They get you praying and settled in the basics before loading you with advanced debates.
They keep your privacy and do not turn your story into content for other people.
They ask about your safety, your family situation, and how you are actually doing.

sections.heading: Warning signs
sections.body: Be careful with anyone who tells you to listen only to them, pushes you to cut everybody off right away, rushes you into marriage or money decisions, asks you to keep a harmful secret, or shames you for wanting qualified help.

sections.heading: Beginner questions should be normal
sections.body: You should be able to ask where to pray, how to make wudu, what a word means, or who could teach you. In a beginner-friendly space, none of those questions turn into an embarrassment.

sections.heading: Referral is a strength
sections.body: A responsible mentor does not pretend to have every answer. Marriage, divorce, abuse, trauma, detailed fiqh, legal problems, clinical distress, and money decisions all belong with qualified people.

sections.heading: If a space feels unsafe
sections.body: Leave if you can do that safely. Then contact someone you trust, another masjid, a community leader, or a professional support service. Staying in an unhealthy setting proves nothing about your sincerity.

scripts.title: Asking where a rule comes from
scripts.body: Thanks for explaining. Is that a religious requirement, a recommendation, or a local custom? And who could I ask for a proper answer?

scripts.title: Stepping out of pressure
scripts.body: I need to slow down and ask someone qualified before I decide that. I'm not comfortable being pushed.

scripts.title: Looking for another space
scripts.body: I don't think this is the right fit for me right now. Do you know another class or masjid that's calm with new Muslims?

scenarios.title: Someone shares your conversion story without permission.
scenarios.response: Ask them to stop, and to take it down if it is posted somewhere. Your privacy still counts even when people are excited for you.

scenarios.title: People overload you with rules.
scenarios.response: Ask for the beginner order: what matters this week, what can wait, and who can teach you steadily.

scenarios.title: A group discourages you from asking other teachers.
scenarios.response: Treat that as a warning sign. Sound learning can survive a second qualified opinion.

title: Halal living in daily life
description: Start with the clear basics of halal food, handle family meals, social events and work calmly, and know when a detail needs local help.
intro: You learn halal living one ordinary decision at a time. Start with the clear basics, try not to slide into checking every label twice, and ask qualified local help when the details get complicated.
summary: Start with the clear lines: no pork, no alcohol, and halal meat where you can get it.
Vegetarian food, seafood, dairy, eggs, beans, and simple cooking at home make the early choices easier.
Ingredients, certification, medicines, and shared kitchen questions vary by place, so they need local guidance.
This is meant to make obedience steadier, not to turn your week into constant worry.

sections.heading: Food basics first
sections.body: Start with choices that are clear and easy to repeat. Nobody expects you to understand every additive on your first grocery run.
items: Avoid pork and alcohol.
Buy halal-certified meat where you can.
Order vegetarian or seafood when you are eating with a group and cannot tell.
Keep a short list of easy meals you can make again and again.

sections.heading: Social events
sections.body: Tell the host what you need before the event if you can. Keep it short and grateful. One calm sentence usually works better than a debate about halal detail.

sections.heading: Family meals
sections.body: Food carries a lot of family history, so a refusal can land harder than you meant it to. If someone feels rejected, reassure them and keep your boundary anyway. Offer to bring a dish, cook alongside them, or pick something everyone at the table can eat.

sections.heading: Work and school
sections.body: For lunches, catered meetings, and work trips, pick the clear option or bring your own. If an event is built around drinking, decide beforehand how much of it you will attend, and ask someone qualified if you are unsure.

sections.heading: When the details need help
sections.body: Gelatin, enzymes, flavorings, medicines, restaurant kitchens, and certification standards get confusing fast. If one of them keeps coming up for you, ask a local imam, a halal certifier, a pharmacist, or a qualified teacher, whichever fits the question.

scripts.title: For a host
scripts.body: Thanks for having me. I eat halal now, so no pork and no alcohol. Vegetarian or seafood is usually easiest, and I'm happy to bring something too.

scripts.title: At work
scripts.body: I have a religious dietary restriction, so no pork and no alcohol. If that makes catering awkward, I'm glad to bring my own lunch.

scripts.title: Asking about an ingredient
scripts.body: This ingredient keeps coming up for me. Could you help me understand the local halal standard without me turning it into an obsession?

scenarios.title: Your family cooks pork in a shared kitchen.
scenarios.response: Keep the ask practical: separate utensils where that is possible, your own pan, or a simple alternative. If the home situation is complicated, ask locally.

scenarios.title: A friend says one bite does not matter.
scenarios.response: Stay calm and say your line again. You are not required to defend the whole religion over dinner.

scenarios.title: You are checking labels for hours.
scenarios.response: That is a sign to simplify. Ask a qualified teacher for a beginner standard, and look at mental health support if the anxiety is taking over.

title: Modesty and clothing
description: Take clothing steps you can keep, around work, school, family, safety, and the weather.
intro: Modesty covers more than clothes, and a change of clothes is still the part everyone notices. This page helps you take it seriously without panic and without dressing up as somebody else's culture.
summary: Understand what modesty is for before you buy a new wardrobe.
Ask a qualified teacher what is required and which details can wait.
A visible change touches family, work, school, safety, and the weather, so plan it.
A style of dress can be beautiful and still not be required of every Muslim.

sections.heading: Start gradually
sections.body: Pick one step you can keep: looser clothing, outfits you can pray in, longer layers, or better coverage in the settings where that is safe. Skip the panic shopping spree.

sections.heading: Culture and religious principle
sections.body: Muslim cultures dress differently from each other. When you see a detail, ask whether it is a requirement, a recommendation, or a local custom. You can respect the culture without mistaking it for a universal rule.

sections.heading: Work and school realities
sections.body: Uniforms, safety gear, sports, labs, and school policy all need planning. Some places publish human rights guidance covering religious dress and accommodation, but the rules differ by location. This page is not legal advice.

sections.heading: Family and safety
sections.body: If a visible change could set off hostility, threats, being thrown out, or someone watching your movements, talk to trusted local support before you move quickly. Planning for your safety is not a shortage of sincerity.

sections.heading: Climate and comfort
sections.body: Heat, cold, mobility, sensory needs, and health conditions all count. Ask a qualified teacher about your own situation and choose clothing that lets you pray and get through your day.

scripts.title: Asking a teacher
scripts.body: I'm new and I want to get modesty right. What's required of me, what can wait, and how should I handle my work and family situation?

scripts.title: Answering pressure
scripts.body: I am taking modesty seriously. I also need to learn it properly and take steps I can actually keep.

scripts.title: At work or school
scripts.body: I have a religious clothing need and I'd like to find a practical way to meet it that still fits the safety and role requirements.

scenarios.title: Someone says your clothes prove you are not sincere.
scenarios.response: Do not let shame set your pace. Ask a qualified, kind teacher what the priorities are and keep moving steadily.

scenarios.title: Your workplace has uniform rules.
scenarios.response: Work out exactly what the religious need is, then take it to the right office or advisor and ask about practical options. Get local legal advice if you hit a wall.

scenarios.title: Family reaction may be unsafe.
scenarios.response: Plan with trusted support before you make a sudden visible change. Your safety comes first.

title: How to ask for help
description: Pick the right person, explain the situation clearly, and know when something needs urgent help.
intro: You do not need to know the right door before you knock. This page helps you work out whether your question belongs with an imam, a teacher, a counselor, a masjid administrator, a rights office, or an emergency service. If you would like to ask our own team, or ask for a mentor, use the Get help page.
summary: Different questions need different people: religious, clinical, legal, safety, administrative, or financial.
A short written summary makes it much easier for someone to answer responsibly.
Sensitive things need a private conversation with someone qualified, not a quick answer in a hallway.
Immediate danger, thoughts of self-harm, abuse, or a medical emergency go to emergency or crisis services first.

sections.heading: Who to ask
items: Ask an imam or a scholar about worship, halal and haram, religious questions in the family, and what to put first.
Ask a teacher or mentor about what to study, Arabic terms you keep hearing, classes, and how to find your way around the community.
Ask a mental health professional about anxiety, depression, trauma, panic, grief, or the risk of a crisis.
Ask a masjid administrator about prayer times, which entrance to use, classes, parking, accessibility, and who to contact.
Ask a rights office or a legal professional about work, school, housing, documents, and legal obligations.

sections.heading: What to include
sections.body: Write down what happened, what you need to decide, where you live, any deadline you are working to, and what is at risk. Keep the private details short unless they change the answer.

sections.heading: Ask for the next step, not the whole map
sections.body: A lot of new Muslims get buried because they ask for everything at once. Ask for the next sensible step, what can wait, and who should look at it if it falls outside what this person does.

sections.heading: When to escalate
sections.body: If someone might hurt you, if you might hurt yourself, if you are being abused, if a child is unsafe, or if there is a medical emergency, contact emergency services or crisis support before you wait on ordinary community advice. In Canada, call 911 in an emergency, or call or text 9-8-8 in a mental health crisis.

sections.heading: If the first person cannot help
sections.body: That does not mean nobody can. Ask them to refer you: another masjid, a scholar, a counselor, a chaplain, a helpline, a public office, or another qualified professional.

scripts.title: A general request
scripts.body: I'm a new Muslim and I'm trying to work out the right next step. It's about [brief topic]. Who should I be asking?

scripts.title: Asking for a private appointment
scripts.body: This is sensitive and it may involve family, safety, or a personal ruling. Could I book a private time, or be referred to someone qualified?

scripts.title: A question for the office
scripts.body: I'm planning my first visit. Could you tell me which entrance to use, the prayer time, anything I should know about parking or accessibility, and whether there's a contact for new Muslims?

scenarios.title: You are embarrassed by a basic question.
scenarios.response: Just say you are new. Responsible teachers expect beginner questions and can usually give you the next step in a sentence.

scenarios.title: You receive opposite answers.
scenarios.response: Ask a qualified local scholar what applies to you, and whether the difference is a valid difference of opinion, a local practice, or a misunderstanding.

scenarios.title: You need help tonight.
scenarios.response: Use urgent help: emergency services, a crisis line, a shelter, a hospital, or someone you trust who can sit with you now.

title: Guide for mentors of new Muslims
description: How to welcome a new Muslim with calm priorities, clear boundaries, and honest referrals.
intro: A mentor does not have to answer everything. The best early support is steady, private, and practical, and it hands the sensitive questions to people who are qualified for them.
summary: Start with a welcome, the basics of prayer, one connection in the community, and a clear sense of what can wait.
Do not turn someone's conversion into public content without clear permission.
Do not bury them in advanced debates, culture wars, or your own preferences.
Send marriage, safety, trauma, clinical distress, legal, financial, and detailed fiqh questions to qualified people.

sections.heading: The first meeting
sections.body: Welcome them, ask what they need today, and keep the conversation calm. What they need might be help with prayer, a tour of the masjid, a class they can trust, support with family, or just one safe person to ask basic questions.
items: Ask before you hand over a long list of tasks.
Give one or two next steps, not twenty.
Tell them how to reach you and how quickly you actually reply.
Keep it private unless they clearly want public support.

sections.heading: What to leave out
sections.body: In a first meeting, skip the sect debates, the online controversy of the week, marriage pressure, politics, comments about their culture, and long lists of optional practices.

sections.heading: Boundaries when you follow up
sections.body: Be reliable without becoming controlling. Do not demand constant updates, keep tabs on their private life, or set yourself up as their only source of guidance.

sections.heading: Where to refer
items: A scholar or imam for personal rulings, marriage, divorce, the details of worship, and religious questions about family.
A clinician or crisis line for trauma, panic, depression, thoughts of self-harm, addiction, or distress that will not lift.
A safety service for abuse, threats, stalking, the risk of losing housing, or someone holding their documents.
A legal or rights professional for work, school, housing, custody, immigration, and anything involving legal or financial paperwork.
A masjid administrator for classes, parking, accessibility, prayer times, and the practical side of visiting.

sections.heading: Privacy and safety
sections.body: A public Shahada, an announcement in the group chat, a photo, or a testimonial can be a lovely moment for the community and a dangerous one for the person. Ask first, every time, and take a no without making them feel guilty for it.

sections.heading: After someone takes Shahada: the handoff
sections.body: The first days after Shahada set the tone. Your job is not to teach everything at once. It is to make sure the person leaves with one trusted contact and one clear next step.
items: In the first hour, congratulate them quietly and ask whether they want privacy, one quiet witness, or an introduction to the community.
Before anyone announces anything, check whether family, housing, work, or safety concerns make it risky for people to know.
Never post photos, videos, or the moment itself without their clear permission.
On the first day, write down one trusted contact together: an imam, a mentor, a new Muslim class, or a Muslim friend.
Share one beginner resource rather than a pile of links, and offer help with wudu and the shape of the prayer.
In the first week, help them pick a gentle plan for learning to pray, and invite them to one community moment such as a class, a prayer, or a meal.
Before you send them to a class or masjid, check that it is actually welcoming to beginners.
Keep check-ins short: one question, one resource, one next step. Tell them plainly what can wait until a teacher goes through it with them.
Do not become their only support, and do not make cultural habits sound like religious obligations.

sections.heading: Where a mentor stops and refers
sections.body: Some questions are not yours to answer, however well you mean. It is fine to say "I don't want to guess about that" and then help them reach someone qualified.
items: Questions about marriage, divorce, custody, inheritance, or conversion certificates go to a qualified local scholar, and to a lawyer or official agency when rights or documents are involved.
If they fear violence, losing their housing, stalking, or retaliation from family, bring in trusted safety services first. Do not encourage them to tell anyone until safety has been thought through.

If they mention suicide or self-harm, cannot keep themselves safe, or are panicking to the point of not functioning, help them call or text 988, or call 911 in an emergency, and reach clinical care. Do not try to counsel a crisis on your own.

Questions about whether a prayer counts, missed prayers, fasting exemptions, zakat, purity details, or disability accommodations go to a qualified scholar, imam, or teacher who can ask follow-up questions.
Hard questions about suffering, qadar, hellfire, or doubts picked up from online clips need a reliable teacher or a structured class that can answer them gradually.
Immigration, workplace, school, and ID questions go to a licensed legal professional, a public rights agency, or a local settlement service.

scripts.title: First welcome
scripts.body: Welcome, I'm really glad you're here. What would help you most this week: prayer basics, a class, a visit to the masjid, something with your family, or just someone to answer beginner questions?

scripts.title: Naming the limit of your help
scripts.body: I can help you with the basics and with finding your way around here, but this one needs a qualified imam, a counselor, or another professional. I can help you find the right person.

scripts.title: Slowing things down
scripts.body: You don't need to learn all of this today. Let's pick one next step and leave the rest for later.

scenarios.title: The new Muslim asks a marriage or divorce question.
scenarios.response: Do not improvise. Help them get private time with a qualified local imam, and with a counselor or lawyer if the situation calls for it.

scenarios.title: They disclose family threats or abuse.
scenarios.response: Safety comes first. Help them reach emergency services, a crisis line, a shelter, or a professional rather than treating it as a normal religious question.

scenarios.title: Community members want to celebrate publicly.
scenarios.response: Ask the new Muslim privately whether they want that. If they say no, or hesitate at all, keep it private.

videos.title: The Prophet's prayer according to authentic hadith
videos.note: For mentors. This is a long, detailed and stricter presentation from one approach, and it differs from some schools on several points. It is useful background for you, but it is not a beginner's starting point. For someone new, start with the salah companion and its shorter videos.

title: Holidays and family occasions
description: What you can join at Christmas, Thanksgiving, birthdays and other family occasions, and how to keep family ties.
intro: Holidays can be the hardest part of the first year. Your family wants you there, and you want to keep your faith. Scholars agree on two things: keeping ties with your family is part of Islam, and a Muslim does not join in another religion's worship. Between those two points they differ, and this guide shows the range of views without choosing for you.
summary: Keeping ties with your family is part of Islam, whatever their religion (Quran 31:14-15 and 60:8).
Sharing a family meal is different from joining religious rites such as a church service or prayers.
Scholars differ on how far to join in each occasion. Each section below names views on both sides so you can ask a teacher which to follow.
If a family visit could put you at risk, your safety comes first.

sections.heading: The principle: family ties, not shared worship
sections.body:
The Quran tells believers to honour their parents. Even if parents push you to worship other than Allah, you do not obey them in that, but you still "keep their company in this world courteously" (Quran 31:15, translation of meaning). It also says Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with people who have not fought you or driven you from your homes (Quran 60:8). When Asma bint Abi Bakr asked whether to keep good relations with her non-Muslim mother, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, "Yes, keep good relation with her" (Sahih al-Bukhari 2620).

The line scholars draw is worship. A SeekersGuidance answer says a Muslim should not actively celebrate another religion's religious festival, and at family gatherings should quietly step out of religious activities. A meal, a visit, or helping in the kitchen is ordinary family time, not worship.

sections.heading: Christmas and Christmas Eve
sections.body:
More lenient view: a SeekersGuidance answer from the Hanafi school (Waseem Hussain, checked by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani) says attending a family Christmas gathering is permitted as part of keeping family ties, as long as you discreetly stay out of religious activities. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta says that accepting invitations to attend such celebrations does not mean acknowledging the beliefs behind them.

Stricter view: the Islamweb Fatwa Center says to keep ties through visits and other permissible means, but not to join the festivities themselves. An AMJA scholar, Dr. Main Khalid Al-Qudah, advises apologising and declining a friend's Christmas Eve dinner invitation because it is a religious occasion (AMJA 77225).

Whatever view you follow, stepping out of prayers or a church service is something all of these answers share.

sections.heading: Gifts and greetings
sections.body:
Gifts: a SeekersGuidance answer says accepting presents from family, neighbours and co-workers is fine because it is a social custom, and giving presents in December to strengthen family ties is permitted if done in your own dignified way. An AMJA scholar, Dr. Hatem al-Haj, calls accepting gifts a sunnah and says you may decline a gift tied directly to a religious ritual (AMJA 1533). SeekersGuidance also advises not keeping a Christmas tree in a Muslim's own home.

Greetings: Egypt's Dar al-Ifta allows congratulating non-Muslims on their occasions, especially family and colleagues, as long as it does not mean agreeing with their beliefs. Shaykh Jamaal Zarabozo, himself a convert, advises not saying "Merry Christmas" and answering warmly in another way, such as "So how have you been?" or "I hope to see you again soon" (AMJA 85952).

sections.heading: Thanksgiving
sections.body:
More lenient view: Shaykh Faraz Rabbani (SeekersGuidance) says attending a Thanksgiving dinner with immediate family is permitted, since it is not an explicitly religious function, especially when there is benefit in going and harm in staying away. Ustadh Farid Dingle (SeekersGuidance) says national or cultural holidays are fine as long as you do not treat them as religiously sacred.

Stricter view: Dr. Main Khalid Al-Qudah of AMJA says Thanksgiving is historically a Christian holiday, so Muslims do not celebrate it, and he treats Mother's Day and Father's Day the same way (AMJA 76974 and 22994).

If you go, eat what is halal for you and politely skip any alcohol.

sections.heading: Halloween
sections.body:
Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, answering a parent in Canada, says that given Halloween's pagan origins, many North American scholars advise not taking part. He suggests giving your children treats or taking them somewhere special instead, and checking with local scholars. Dr. Hatem al-Haj of AMJA, answering a convert mother who wanted to share her own childhood fun, suggests putting that candy-sharing and dressing up into the two Eids (AMJA 83012).

We did not find a scholarly source that permits taking part, so we cannot show a more lenient view here. Some scholars treat handing out candy at the door as a separate question, so ask a local scholar about that. It is fine to feel a little sad about letting go of something you loved. Building new family traditions around the Eids helps.

sections.heading: Birthdays
sections.body:
More lenient view: Dr. Main Khalid Al-Qudah of AMJA says birthdays are not part of Islamic tradition, but people treat them as social occasions, so they are not among the explicitly forbidden matters and an occasional celebration, especially for children, is no harm (AMJA 77128). Dr. Hatem al-Haj of AMJA encourages a convert parent to celebrate non-religious occasions such as birthdays and exam results with her children (AMJA 1533).

Stricter view: Dr. Salah Al-Sawy of AMJA says it is not permissible to celebrate birthdays or to accept invitations to birthday parties (AMJA 22801). A SeekersGuidance teacher, Dr. Muhammad Fayez Awad, sets out both views and leans towards prohibition.

sections.heading: Easter, church services, weddings and funerals
sections.body:
An Easter or Christmas church service is worship, and that is where scholars draw a clear line. A SeekersGuidance answer (Ustadh Farid Dingle) says it is not permissible to actively celebrate another religion's religious festival, while learning about other traditions is fine. An Easter family lunch is treated like the Christmas meal above.

Church weddings and funerals have a wider range of views. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and an AMJA scholar allow attending a relative's funeral, even in a church. SeekersGuidance Hanafi answers allow the family gathering but not the church service without a strong need. IslamQA takes a strict view, including on church weddings. Our core beliefs topic explains why worship belongs to Allah alone. Ask a local imam before the event, because the details of your situation matter.

sections.heading: Parties where alcohol is served
sections.body:
A hadith in Jami at-Tirmidhi (2801, graded Hasan by Darussalam on Sunnah.com) is the basis for many scholars advising against sitting at a table where alcohol is served. A SeekersGuidance answer about a family birthday party with alcohol advises politely declining a gathering centred on alcohol and offering an alternative, such as taking the family out for a meal or visiting beforehand.

Scholars differ on events where alcohol is present but is not the point of the gathering, such as a New Year's dinner. Ask your imam how this applies to you.

sections.heading: Food at family meals
sections.body:
Pork and alcohol are the clear things to avoid. Meat is where views differ: some scholars accept the meat of Christians and Jews under Quran 5:5, and many others and many Canadian certifiers accept only zabiha meat. You do not need to settle this at the dinner table. Many converts take the vegetarian dishes, fish or sides, or bring a halal dish to share.

If your family cooks pork in a shared kitchen, a SeekersGuidance answer from the Hanafi school says washing dishes and pans, even once, removes the impurity. Our FAQ has more on food questions.

sections.heading: Your first December
sections.body: If this season feels lonely, you are not alone. In a 2025 Yaqeen Institute survey of 618 converts in the United States, about 40% said they felt lonely during Ramadan and 42% on Eid. Plan something for yourself too: visit Muslim friends, go to a masjid event, or invite your family to your Eid in return. Dr. Jonathan Brown, who became Muslim at 19, writes about keeping up his family's Christmas gatherings and wishing he had hidden his faith less.

sections.heading: If your family is hostile
sections.body: If a holiday visit could lead to shouting, threats or violence, your safety comes first. A SeekersGuidance answer says you may reduce contact with a harmful relative and keep the tie in other ways, such as calls, small gifts and making dua for them. The Government of Canada's safety planning page can help you plan, and in danger you should call 911. Our red flags and staying safe guide and our family and friends guide have more help.

scripts.title: Joining the meal
scripts.body: I'm so glad to be here with you all. I'll sit out the prayer, but I wouldn't miss dinner.

scripts.title: Declining the church service
scripts.body: I love you and I'll be there for lunch. I won't come to the service, because I pray differently now.

scripts.title: Asking about food
scripts.body: Can I bring a halal dish so there's something I can eat too? I'd love to make my part of the meal.

scripts.title: Turning down a drink
scripts.body: I don't drink, but I'll bring dessert.

scripts.title: Saying no to Halloween
scripts.body: We're not doing trick-or-treating this year, but we've got treats at home and a special outing planned.

scripts.title: Inviting your family back
scripts.body: Would you like to come over for Eid? I'd love you to see what it's like.

scenarios.title: Your mother cries when you say you won't come to the Christmas service.
scenarios.response: Stay gentle. Tell her you still want to spend Christmas with her, and offer to come for the meal or to visit the next day. Hurt feelings often soften once your family sees you keep turning up.

scenarios.title: Your child's class is holding a Halloween party.
scenarios.response: The scholars whose answers we checked advise not joining Halloween, and suggest treats or an outing instead. You can talk to the teacher about an alternative, and ask a local scholar about your situation.

scenarios.title: A coworker hands you a Christmas gift.
scenarios.response: Accepting a gift is widely considered fine, and one AMJA scholar calls it a sunnah. Say thank you warmly.

title: Red flags and staying safe
description: How to spot pressure, money requests and scams in a community, and where to report them in Canada.
intro: Most people you meet at a masjid or in a convert group are kind and want to help. A few are not. This guide lists the warning signs that come up most for new Muslims, what to do about them, and where to report in Canada. Being targeted is never your fault.
summary: Nobody has the right to ask a new Muslim for money, rush you into marriage, or tell you to keep secrets.
If you are in danger right now, call 911.
Women can call Sakeenah Canada's 24/7 hotline at 1-888-671-3446 or the Nisa Helpline at +1 888 711 6472.
Report scams to your local police and to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501 or reportcyberandfraud.canada.ca.
You can report a mentor or group connected to Revert Guide through our get help page.

sections.heading: Warning signs to take seriously
sections.body: One of these on its own does not prove someone means harm. Two or three together are a good reason to slow down and talk to someone you trust.
items: Someone asks you for money, a loan, or a donation for a cause, especially in cash, gift cards or cryptocurrency.
Someone pushes you to marry quickly, or offers to introduce you to someone to marry before you are ready.
Someone you have not met in person says they love you, wants to move the chat somewhere private, and always has a reason not to meet.
A person or group tells you to keep things secret from your family, your friends or other teachers.
A group says most Muslims are not real Muslims, tells you to cut off your family, or talks about anger and violence.
Someone offers help with immigration or sponsorship and promises a guaranteed or faster result.

sections.heading: Money requests and charity
sections.body:
The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns about people who ask for donations to a charity, association or religious cause, often with a lot of pressure. The Canada Revenue Agency says not to give if you feel pushed to give right away.

If you want to give, give to a registered charity rather than to a person. Ask for the charity's details in writing and for its registration number, then check it on the CRA list of charities or by calling 1-800-267-2384. Registered charities do not accept cryptocurrency, and cash and gift cards cannot be traced. If money collected at a masjid or an event does not add up, you can report a registered charity to the Canada Revenue Agency.

sections.heading: Pressure to marry, and romance scams
sections.body:
Marriage is a big decision, and it is fine to take time to settle into your faith first. You can say no, or not yet. A sincere person will be patient, and glad for your family, friends or a trusted imam to be involved.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre lists these signs of a romance scam: someone you have not met professes their love, wants to move quickly to a private app such as WhatsApp, always has an excuse not to meet, gets upset to guilt you into sending money, and discourages you from talking about them with friends and family. Never send money or personal documents to someone you have not met in person.

The Anti-Fraud Centre also warns about sextortion, where a fake profile asks for intimate video and then demands money. Live video can be recorded. Do not send money, and report it to the police and the Anti-Fraud Centre.

sections.heading: Immigration and sponsorship offers
sections.body:
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) says no one can guarantee you a visa or faster processing. IRCC will never ask you to pay into a personal bank account, send money through a private transfer service, contact you from a free email address such as Gmail, ask for payment by phone, or start a conversation on social media. Scammers also phone pretending to be IRCC and threaten deportation unless you pay.

If you are unsure, contact IRCC directly. For your own case, speak to a licensed immigration lawyer or consultant. IRCC's reporting page explains where to report a scam.

sections.heading: Groups that isolate you
sections.body:
Be careful with any group that cuts you off from your family, other teachers and the wider community, asks you to keep secrets, looks down on most other Muslims, or stirs up anger and talk of violence. Public Safety Canada says violent extremism is not linked to any particular religion. It also describes online recruiters (its example is Daesh) who isolate people from positive influences and then move them to more private platforms.

If you are worried about a group, step back and talk to a trusted imam, friend or family member. If someone talks about violence or you feel unsafe, call 911. Public Safety Canada lists free, voluntary support programmes, such as ETA in the GTA and Southern Ontario (call or text 416-617-4561) and Project ReSet in Ottawa (613-789-7418).

sections.heading: If you are keeping your conversion private
sections.body:
When to tell people is your decision, and many converts wait for the right time. If someone at home might look at your phone or computer, remember that installed apps, browser history and messages can be seen. The Government of Canada's safety planning page warns that someone can monitor your online activity, and that there is no sure way to delete all of that information.

This site can be installed on your phone and keeps pages for offline reading, so it may show up in your apps or history. Private browsing avoids history but not an installed app. Use a strong, unique password and turn on two-step sign-in for your accounts. If you are afraid of violence at home, the same government page walks you through making a safety plan. In danger, call 911.

sections.heading: Support for women
sections.body: If you are a woman facing pressure at home, abuse, or the risk of losing your housing, these Muslim women's services in Canada can help. We checked each number on the service's own website on 23 September 2026. In immediate danger, call 911 first.
items: Sakeenah Canada: 24/7 hotline 1-888-671-3446 for women and children fleeing domestic violence. Sakeenah also runs transitional homes in several cities. Checked 23 September 2026.
Nisa Helpline: +1 888 711 6472, 7 days a week from 8 am to midnight Eastern, for women and girls 14 and up. It is free, confidential peer support, not a crisis line.
Nisa Homes, run by the Nisa Foundation: safe shelter for women and children, with locations across Canada. You can apply for help through nisafoundation.ca.
If you are thinking about suicide, or worried about someone, call or text 9-8-8 at any time.

sections.heading: How to report
sections.body: The police investigate crimes. The Anti-Fraud Centre collects reports and helps police spot patterns, so it is worth reporting to both.
items: In immediate danger, or if a crime is happening now: call 911.

A crime that is not an emergency, such as theft, threats or fraud: call your local police non-emergency line or use its online reporting. For example, Ottawa Police is 613-236-1222, and the OPP is 1-888-310-1122 in areas it polices.

Scams and fraud: tell your local police first, then report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre online at reportcyberandfraud.canada.ca or by phone at 1-888-495-8501 (Monday to Friday, 10 am to 4:45 pm Eastern, closed on holidays). Online reports can be anonymous.
A child at risk: in Ontario, everyone is required by law to report it to a children's aid society.
Misuse of a registered charity's money: report it to the Canada Revenue Agency.
A mentor, group or volunteer connected to Revert Guide: tell us through our get help page.

sections.heading: Being targeted is not your fault
sections.body: The Anti-Fraud Centre says fraud can happen to anyone, and scammers often go after kind, trusting people. Being targeted says nothing about your faith or your intelligence. Stopping, asking questions and reporting are all the right things to do, and a healthy community will back you.

scripts.title: Saying no to a money request
scripts.body: I don't give money to individuals. If this is for a registered charity, send me its name and registration number and I'll look into it.

scripts.title: Slowing down a marriage conversation
scripts.body: I'm not ready to talk about marriage yet. I'm still settling into my faith, and when I am ready I'll involve my family or an imam I trust.

scripts.title: Stepping back from a group
scripts.body: I need space to learn at my own pace and to ask other teachers too. Please respect that.

scenarios.title: Someone you met at the masjid asks to borrow money.
scenarios.response: You never have to lend or give money. Say no kindly. If it keeps happening, tell someone you trust at the masjid office.

scenarios.title: An online contact wants to marry you and asks for money for a plane ticket.
scenarios.response: These are romance scam signs listed by the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. Stop sending money or documents, and report it to your local police and the Anti-Fraud Centre.

scenarios.title: A mentor asks you to keep your meetings secret.
scenarios.response: A real mentor does not ask for secrecy. Stop meeting them, and report it to the programme they belong to, or to us through the get help page if they are connected to Revert Guide.

title: How mentoring works and our conduct standards
description: How mentors are vetted and trained, what they promise, how matching and check-ins work, and how to report a concern.
intro: A mentor is a volunteer who helps you with the basics and keeps you company through the first months. This page sets out how we choose mentors, what they promise, and what to do if something goes wrong. It does not name anyone. The standards follow published benchmarks from MENTOR and Volunteer Canada, adapted for adult volunteers.
summary: Every mentor applies in writing, gives two references, has an interview, and is checked with the masjid they belong to.
Mentors sign a code of conduct: no marriage proposals, no money, no recruiting, and your story stays private.
You are matched with a mentor of the same gender by default, and you can say no to any match.
If a mentor breaks the rules, you report it to the coordinators, never to the mentor.

sections.heading: How mentors are vetted
sections.body: Nobody is matched with a new Muslim until they have finished every one of these steps.
items: A written application.
Two references, and we contact both of them.
An interview with a coordinator, in person or by video.
A check with the masjid or Islamic organisation the applicant belongs to.

sections.heading: The code of conduct mentors sign
sections.body: Every mentor signs this before a match. If a mentor breaks it, the coordinators end the match.
items: No marriage proposals, no matchmaking and no romantic contact.
No asking for money, lending money, selling anything or asking you to donate.
No recruiting you into any group, movement, business or paid course.
Your conversion, name, photo and story stay private unless you clearly say otherwise. Mentors do not add you to groups without asking.
Contact stays in the channels and at the times you both agreed. A mentor does not demand constant updates or keep tabs on your private life.
Personal religious rulings go to a qualified imam. Mentors help with the basics and refer the rest.
Men mentor men and women mentor women by default.

sections.heading: Training before the first match
sections.body: Every mentor completes at least two hours of training before they are matched. It covers the code of conduct, boundaries, privacy, when to refer someone to an imam or a professional, and how to report a concern.
items: A Guide to New Muslim Mentoring, a recorded course published by Islamwise on YouTube. The playlist is linked in the sources below.
Our own Guide for mentors of new Muslims, which covers the first meeting, what to leave out, boundaries and where to refer.

sections.heading: How matching works
sections.body:
A coordinator reads your request and looks for a mentor who shares your gender, speaks your language, is in your time zone, and ideally lives near you. Before anyone's contact details are shared, the coordinator tells you about the proposed mentor, and you can say no.

You and your mentor then agree in writing how often you will talk, which channel you will use, what the mentoring covers, and who to contact with a concern.

sections.heading: Check-ins
sections.body: A coordinator checks in with you, not only with your mentor. The first check-in comes after your first conversation, then at least once a month for the first months. That is a good moment to mention anything that is bothering you, however small.

sections.heading: Meeting in person
items: Meet in a public place. A masjid during open hours is best.
Another adult is present as well as your mentor.
No home visits, and no meetings in cars.

sections.heading: Reporting a concern
sections.body: If your mentor asks for money, proposes marriage, pushes you towards a group, shares your story, or makes you uncomfortable in any way, tell the coordinators. The report address is on the Get help page. Your report goes to the coordinators, not to your mentor. If you are in danger, call 911.

sections.heading: What the team is still deciding
sections.body: Two points are not settled yet. Until they are, every standard above still applies in full.
items: Police checks. A police service has to advise whether mentoring adult converts qualifies for a Vulnerable Sector Check. The team will ask and publish the answer. Whatever it is, the application, references, interview and masjid check still apply.
Who approves mentors. The team has not yet named the role that gives final approval. Until it does, nobody is matched without every vetting step completed.

scripts.title: Asking for a mentor
scripts.body: I became Muslim recently and I would like a mentor. I would prefer someone who is a [man or woman], speaks [language], and lives near [city].

scripts.title: Saying no to a match
scripts.body: Thank you for finding someone. I don't think this match is right for me. Could you look for someone else?

scripts.title: Reporting a concern
scripts.body: I want to report something about my mentor. It happened on [date]. This is what they said or did: [short description].

scenarios.title: Your mentor mentions someone they would like you to marry.
scenarios.response: That breaks the code of conduct. You do not have to answer. Tell the coordinators and they will step in.

scenarios.title: Your mentor asks to borrow money or asks you to donate.
scenarios.response: Say no, and report it. A mentor never asks for money. If you already sent money, you can also report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

scenarios.title: Your mentor suggests meeting at their home.
scenarios.response: Suggest the masjid instead. Home visits are not allowed, and you can tell the coordinators it came up.
